title: Numbers 15:1–16
context: After the failure at Kadesh in Numbers 14, where the generation that left Egypt is condemned to die in the wilderness, the LORD gives instructions for life in the land: when you have come into the land. The laws set grain and drink offerings alongside animal sacrifices and insist on one law for native-born and foreigner. Placed here, they quietly reaffirm that God’s promise still stands for the next generation. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks to Moses again, right after Israel’s rebellion and sentence in chapter 14. Arminian readers see God continuing to speak to his people after their failure. His word is not withdrawn because of their sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s faithfulness to his covenant purposes despite Israel’s unbelief. The next generation will still enter the land. Both traditions read this placement as a sign of grace.

verses.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘When you have come into the land of your habitations, which I give to you,
verses.arminianNotes: The instructions begin with a promise: when you come into the land I give you. Arminian readers see hope restored to the children of the condemned generation. God’s promise remains open to those who will trust him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s promise standing firm, even after judgment on many. The land is described as God’s gift. Both traditions read the verse as an assurance of future fulfillment.

verses.text: and will make an offering by fire to the LORD—a burnt offering, or a sacrifice, to accomplish a vow, or as a free will offering, or in your set feasts, to make a pleasant aroma to the LORD, of the herd, or of the flock—
verses.arminianNotes: Various offerings by fire are listed, from vows to freewill gifts and feasts. Arminian readers see a wide range of worship responses, including voluntary devotion. Worship in the land will include gratitude as well as duty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God ordering worship for every occasion. A pleasing aroma describes offerings God accepts. Christians in both traditions read these sacrifices as fulfilled in Christ, as Ephesians 5:2 uses similar language.

verses.text: then he who offers his offering shall offer to the LORD a meal offering of one tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with one fourth of a hin of oil.
verses.arminianNotes: A grain offering with oil accompanies each offering. Arminian readers see the fruit of the land joined to animal sacrifice. Israel’s produce becomes part of worship. The WEB footnotes estimate the ephah and hin; ancient measures are approximate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the whole of Israel’s life, including bread and oil, offered to God. Both traditions read the details as ceremonial instruction for worship in the land.

verses.text: You shall prepare wine for the drink offering, one fourth of a hin, with the burnt offering or for the sacrifice, for each lamb.
verses.arminianNotes: Wine for a drink offering accompanies each lamb. Arminian readers see joy and abundance represented in worship. The wine of the land is poured out before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the drink offering as part of complete worship. Paul uses the drink offering image for his own life in Philippians 2:17. Both traditions share this reading.

verses.text: “ ‘For a ram, you shall prepare for a meal offering two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with the third part of a hin of oil;
verses.arminianNotes: A ram requires a larger grain offering. Arminian readers see offerings scaled to the size of the sacrifice. Worship is proportioned and ordered, not arbitrary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see careful regulation of worship by God’s word. Both traditions read the detail descriptively, without forcing theological meaning onto the measurements. Worship follows God’s pattern.

verses.text: and for the drink offering you shall offer the third part of a hin of wine, of a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: A third of a hin of wine goes with the ram. Arminian readers see the pleasing aroma repeated as the goal of worship. God delights in offerings given as he directs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s acceptance as the aim of sacrifice. Both traditions read the verse as part of shared ceremonial instruction. The aim of every offering is acceptance before God.

verses.text: When you prepare a bull for a burnt offering or for a sacrifice, to accomplish a vow, or for peace offerings to the LORD,
verses.arminianNotes: Instructions follow for a bull offered for a vow or peace offering. Arminian readers see different occasions of worship welcomed. Vows and fellowship offerings expressed gratitude and devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see worship ordered for many circumstances. Both traditions read the verse as introducing the largest offering in the series. The bull is the largest animal in the list, and its offerings are scaled accordingly.

verses.text: then he shall offer with the bull a meal offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with half a hin of oil;
verses.arminianNotes: The bull requires three tenths of an ephah of flour with oil. Arminian readers see offerings growing with the animal’s size. Larger sacrifices call for larger accompanying gifts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see consistency in God’s instructions. Both traditions treat the measurements as ceremonial detail, with modern equivalents only approximate. The pattern of increase continues from lamb to ram to bull.

verses.text: and you shall offer for the drink offering half a hin of wine, for an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Half a hin of wine accompanies the bull. Arminian readers see the series completed with the same aim of a pleasing aroma. Worship is offered wholeheartedly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the completeness of the prescribed offerings. Both traditions share this reading. Grain, oil, wine, and animal together form a full offering made from the produce of the promised land.

verses.text: Thus it shall be done for each bull, for each ram, for each of the male lambs, or of the young goats.
verses.arminianNotes: These rules apply to each bull, ram, lamb, or goat. Arminian readers see consistency in worship across offerings. No sacrifice is left without its accompaniment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see order and uniformity in God’s instructions. Both traditions read the verse as summarizing the preceding regulations. No kind of animal is treated as exempt from the accompanying gifts.

verses.text: According to the number that you shall prepare, so you shall do to everyone according to their number.
verses.arminianNotes: The same procedure applies to each animal according to number. Arminian readers see fairness and consistency in worship. Each offering receives the same care. The rule holds for every sacrifice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s ordered worship applied without exception. Both traditions read the verse as straightforward instruction. Regularity in worship guards against careless or improvised offerings and keeps the whole community on the same footing.

verses.text: “ ‘All who are native-born shall do these things in this way, in offering an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Native-born Israelites shall offer this way. Arminian readers see clear expectations for the covenant community. Worship follows God’s pattern, not personal preference. Belonging to Israel brings both privilege and obligation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the regulation of worship by God’s command. Both traditions share this reading. Israelites by birth have no special exemption from the prescribed form; they too must offer as God directs.

verses.text: If a stranger lives as a foreigner with you, or whoever may be among you throughout your generations, and will offer an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to the LORD, as you do, so he shall do.
verses.arminianNotes: A foreigner who offers must do so the same way. Arminian readers see outsiders welcomed into worship on equal terms. God’s house is open to the stranger who joins Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the inclusion of foreigners anticipating the wider reach of God’s people. Both traditions share this reading. The foreigner who wishes to worship receives the same instructions and the same welcome as the native-born.

verses.text: For the assembly, there shall be one statute for you and for the stranger who lives as a foreigner, a statute forever throughout your generations. As you are, so the foreigner shall be before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: There is one statute for native and foreigner; as you are, so the foreigner is before the LORD. Arminian readers see equal standing before God. The stranger is not a second-class worshiper.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see equality before God within the covenant community. Christians in both traditions see this pointing toward the inclusion of Gentiles in Christ.

verses.text: One law and one ordinance shall be for you and for the stranger who lives as a foreigner with you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: One law and one ordinance apply to all. Arminian readers see the principle repeated for emphasis. God’s law treats insiders and outsiders alike. The repetition underlines the principle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the consistency of God’s justice. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground. The emphasis on one law for all recurs in 15:29 and shows God’s even-handed concern for every worshiper.
